lead: An isolated DC-DC converter puts a transformer between the switch and the load, so the input and output have no direct electrical path. The transformer carries energy by magnetic field, gives safety, allows a large voltage ratio, and can feed several outputs. The flyback stores energy in the transformer during the on-time and delivers it during the off-time. The forward delivers energy during the on-time and resets the core every cycle. Both appear in chargers, standby supplies and industrial DC rails.
prereq: You need: buck converter and buck-boost for duty ratio and output stages, and Unit 1 for device ratings and snubbers.

sections.h3: Why isolation, and the flyback idea

blocks.text: An isolated converter puts a transformer between the switch and the load. There is no direct DC path; energy crosses by magnetic field. Isolation is wanted for safety, for a step-up or step-down too large for one duty ratio, and for several outputs from one primary. The flyback is the simplest isolated converter. Its transformer is really a coupled inductor with an air gap, a small non-magnetic gap in the core. The primary inductance stores energy.

With the switch ON, the input voltage appears across the primary, primary current ramps, and the secondary diode is reverse biased. The core stores energy in its gap. With the switch OFF, the primary voltage reverses, the secondary diode conducts, and the stored energy charges the output capacitor. CCM means the magnetic current never falls to zero in a cycle. blocks.where: V<sub>o</sub> is the output DC voltage; V<sub>s</sub> is the input DC voltage; D is the duty ratio, the fraction of the switching period the switch is on; n = N<sub>1</sub>/N<sub>2</sub> is the primary-to-secondary turns ratio.

blocks.text: The switch in a flyback holds the input voltage plus the reflected output voltage: stress = V<sub>s</sub> + n·V<sub>o</sub>, plus a spike from leakage inductance. Leakage inductance is primary flux that does not link the secondary. An RCD clamp, a resistor-capacitor-diode network, absorbs that spike. Without it the switch may break at turn-off.

sections.h3: Forward converter: energy passes in ON

blocks.text: A forward converter passes energy while the switch is ON. The transformer is a true transformer, not the main energy store. When the switch is ON, primary current flows, the secondary voltage forward-biases the rectifier, and current ramps in output inductor L<sub>o</sub>. When the switch is OFF, a freewheeling diode keeps L<sub>o</sub> current flowing. The output stage is a buck converter after the transformer, so it is smooth and suits medium power.

blocks.where: V<sub>o</sub> is the output DC voltage; V<sub>s</sub> is the input DC voltage; D is the duty ratio; N<sub>2</sub>/N<sub>1</sub> is the secondary-to-primary turns ratio.

blocks.text: The core must be reset every cycle. During ON, magnetizing flux rises. During OFF, it must fall back to the same value. A third reset winding does this. If the reset winding has the same turns as the primary, it applies V<sub>s</sub> in the off-time and takes D·T<sub>s</sub> to reset. That time must fit inside (1 − D)·T<sub>s</sub>, so D must stay below 0.5. If reset is incomplete, flux walks up cycle by cycle, the core saturates, and the switch current spikes. An active clamp can reset the core and allow a wider duty range; only a few universities teach it.

The choice is mostly power level and cost. Flyback is simple and cheap: phone chargers, standby supplies, auxiliary bias rails. It has high peak currents and more output ripple. Forward is for medium power: telecom and industrial DC rails, where a smoother output is worth the extra transformer, reset winding and output inductor. Both need a clamp or snubber for the leakage spike, and both trade a duty limit and isolation against a non-isolated buck.

examples.question: A flyback converter runs from 48 V DC at 100 kHz with a transformer of 40 primary turns and 20 secondary turns, so n = N1/N2 = 2. (a) Find V_o at D = 0.4. (b) Find the duty ratio needed for 12 V output. (c) Find the switch voltage stress, ignoring the leakage spike, at 12 V output and at the 16 V output of part (a).
steps: Turns ratio: n = N1/N2 = 40/20 = 2. Duty ratio D = 0.4, so 1 − D = 0.6.
(b) Put V_o = 12 V: 12 = 48·D / (2(1 − D)). Multiply both sides by 2(1 − D): 24(1 − D) = 48D.
(c) Stress = V_s + n·V_o. At 12 V: 48 + 2 × 12 = 72 V. At 16 V: 48 + 2 × 16 = 80 V. A 150 V device leaves margin.
examples.answer: At D = 0.4, V_o = 16 V; for 12 V, D = 0.3333; the ideal switch stress is 72 V at 12 V output and 80 V at 16 V output, so a 150 V device is sensible.

traps: On a flyback the primary-to-secondary turns ratio n = N1/N2 sits in the denominator of the CCM gain. V_o = V_s·D·(N2/N1) is the forward formula, not the flyback formula.
Forgetting the leakage spike: V_s + n·V_o is only the ideal switch stress. The RCD clamp handles the extra spike, and the device rating must leave margin.
A forward converter with a 1:1 reset winding must keep D below 0.5. Pushing D higher leaves no time to reset the core, so flux walks and the core saturates.
Do not treat the flyback transformer as a true transformer in the energy-transfer sense. It is a coupled inductor; the primary inductance is the energy-storing element.
Duty ratio D is a fraction, not a percentage. Enter 0.4 into the formulas, not 40.

quiz.q: State the CCM gain formula of a flyback converter and define n.
quiz.a: V_o = V_s·D / ((1 − D)·n), where n = N1/N2 is the primary-to-secondary turns ratio.

quiz.q: Why is the secondary diode of a flyback reverse biased during the switch ON time?
quiz.a: During ON the primary is connected to the source and the secondary voltage has the opposite polarity for conduction. The diode blocks, so energy is stored in the primary inductance instead of being delivered.

quiz.q: A flyback has V_s = 24 V, n = N1/N2 = 3 and D = 0.5. Find V_o in CCM.
A forward converter uses a reset winding with the same turns as the primary. Explain why D must stay below 0.5.
quiz.a: The reset winding applies V_s during the off-time. It needs D·T_s to remove the volt-seconds added during the ON time. That must fit in (1 − D)·T_s, giving D below 0.5. Otherwise the core flux walks up and saturates.

quiz.q: Write the ideal gain formula of a forward converter.
quiz.a: V_o = V_s·D·(N2/N1), where N2/N1 is the secondary-to-primary turns ratio.

quiz.q: A forward converter has V_s = 48 V, N2/N1 = 0.25 and D = 0.4. Find V_o.
Why does a flyback need an RCD clamp across the primary switch?
quiz.a: Leakage inductance stores energy that cannot transfer to the secondary. At switch turn-off this energy produces a voltage spike added to V_s + n·V_o. The RCD clamp absorbs the spike and protects the switch.

quiz.q: Why is the flyback transformer often called a coupled inductor?
quiz.a: Because its primary inductance is the main energy-storing element. The core has an air gap to store energy, and energy is stored during ON and delivered during OFF, unlike a true transformer that passes energy during ON.

beyond: Not for the exam. Active-clamp flybacks and GaN-based flybacks now push phone chargers past 100 W in small cases. Planar transformers and integrated synchronous rectifiers reduce height and loss. Search terms: active clamp flyback, QR flyback, forward converter reset, planar magnetics.
